title: Device Driver Discovery
summary: Device driver discovery is the enumeration of the drivers and kernel modules present on a host, usually as a step before choosing an escalation path. A driver list reveals what hardware the machine has, which security products are installed through their filter drivers, whether the host is a real workstation or a virtual machine, and which third party drivers might carry a known vulnerability. On Windows the work is done with the driverquery command line tool, the EnumDeviceDrivers interface, or registry keys that describe installed services; on Linux and macOS the same information comes from the proc and dev filesystems or from tools such as lsmod and modinfo. The activity itself looks benign, which is the detection problem. The useful signal is context: driver enumeration by a user or script with no administrative task to perform, appearing shortly after a foothold and shortly before a privilege escalation attempt.

beginner.definition: Device drivers are small programs that let the operating system talk to hardware and to security tools. Discovering drivers means listing all of them on a computer. An attacker does this to learn what the machine is and where a weakness might be.
beginner.whyItMatters: A driver list tells an attacker a great deal in one command. They learn which security products are running, which helps them avoid those tools. They learn whether the machine is a virtual test system or a real one. They also spot old drivers that could be abused to gain higher privileges. Because the command looks normal, defenders must judge it by context rather than by the tool alone.
howItWorks: The attacker gains a foothold and wants to understand the machine before acting further.
They run a built in command such as driverquery, or call a system interface that lists drivers.
On Linux or macOS they read kernel module lists with tools such as lsmod or modinfo.
They review the output for security products, unusual hardware, or virtual machine markers.
They pick out old or vulnerable drivers that might allow them to gain higher privileges.
They use what they learned to choose the next step, such as a specific escalation attempt.
beginner.example: Imagine a burglar who slips into an office at night. Before touching anything, they walk to the wall where the fuse box and alarm panel are labelled. One label says the alarm is an old model. Another shows the cameras sit on a separate circuit. Nothing is broken yet, and no alarm has sounded. The burglar is simply reading the building to plan the next move. Device driver discovery is that stroll along the wall. The list of drivers tells the attacker which defences are present. It also shows which old equipment could be turned against the building.
takeaways: Driver and kernel module lists reveal security products and possible weaknesses.
A normal command can still be suspicious when the user has no reason to run it.
Judge discovery activity by what happened just before and just after it.

objectives: Explain what a device driver is and why a list of them is valuable to an attacker.
Name the built in tools that enumerate drivers on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
Describe how driver information helps an attacker plan privilege escalation.
Explain why this activity is hard to detect without surrounding context.
Identify the log sources that record discovery command execution.
